content: Hospital separation refers to the event when a patient or resident departs from a healthcare facility. This can occur due to various reasons, including death, discharge, leaving against medical advice, or being transferred to another facility. The number of separations is the most commonly utilized metric to assess the usage of hospital services. This measure is preferred over admissions because hospital abstracts for inpatient care are typically based on data collected at the time of discharge. Hospital separations are one of the key indicators used to evaluate morbidity when assessing the burden of a disease. Another important factor considered in this context is the length of hospital stay. The most common reasons for hospital separations include the following conditions: 1. Digestive system disorders. 2. Neoplasms (tumors, both benign and malignant). 3. Injuries or poisoning. 4. Pregnancy and childbirth-related conditions. 5. Musculoskeletal diseases. 6. Genitourinary diseases. 7. Respiratory diseases. In terms of the length of hospital stay, the conditions associated with the longest to shortest durations are as follows: 1. Mental and behavioral disorders, such as schizophrenia, delusional disorders, and mood disorders. 2. Diseases of the circulatory system. 3. Neoplasms. 4. Injuries or poisoning.
